source.title: Unveiling Scaling Behaviors in Molecular Language Models: Effects of Model Size, Data, and Representation
source.authors: Dong Xu; Qihua Pan; Si-Si Yuan; Jian-Qiang Li; Ze-Xuan Zhu; Jun-Kai Ji

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some downstream figure labels and plotted values are garbled in the extracted text; the paper also contains inconsistent SAFE allocation results.
record.tranche_reason: It investigates scaling behavior in molecular language models, a new training and representation setting, using held-out pretraining cross-entropy and compute-controlled sweeps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own pretraining-loss, compute-optimal-allocation, and downstream-scale findings. Detailed downstream bar-plot values in Figures 13–21 are not reliably readable in the extracted text, so rows use only the paper's explicit summaries. Cited results from earlier molecular and natural-language scaling studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own grid of decoder-only molecular-string LMs: 5 representations × 8 sizes (1M–650M) × 4 token budgets (100M–3B), from scratch. It fits a bivariate power law to held-out cross-entropy and derives compute-optimal allocation. It also measures LoRA downstream performance across pretraining scale. This is a new setting (molecular strings) with its own results bearing on V1, V3, V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is mostly right. The authors further claim molecular LMs follow compute-optimal scaling laws analogous to NLP, that representation fundamentally shapes those laws, and that pretraining scaling trends 'reliably transfer' to downstream tasks. That last claim is stronger than their own Tox21/SIDER results support. They also argue that saturated de novo metrics and optimization-dominated benchmarks explain earlier negative findings.
record.recipe_differences: Uses from-scratch molecular string-model grids, token-averaged validation cross-entropy, and a fitted bivariate loss law under an approximate P·D compute constraint; also varies molecular representation and evaluates LoRA transfer. It is not a reproduction of the original natural-language experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Molecular representation changes loss levels and reported compute-optimal allocation trends. Repeated passes over a fixed corpus show diminishing gains and mild fluctuations. Downstream trends vary by task and representation.
record.problems: The paper reports no independent empirical check of its extrapolated loss predictions beyond the training grid. SAFE's compute-optimal ratio direction conflicts between the main text/Table 3 and Appendix Table 4. Detailed downstream plot values are not reliably readable in the supplied extraction, and the primary loss fits use single-epoch runs.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed downstream scale-by-size-by-token-budget bars from Figures 13–21 were not split into individual rows because their plotted values are garbled in the supplied text; explicit task-level summaries are recorded in R12–R21. Comparative SOTA tables were omitted because they do not report scale trends.

untested.parts: Natural-language text. Model sizes beyond 650M and token budgets beyond 3B. Parameter range spans under 3 orders, tokens only 1.5 orders.
Extrapolated frontier segments are plotted but never checked against larger runs.
Fitted optima are not validated with new runs. Natural-language allocation (Kaplan vs Hoffmann) is not tested. The power-of-compute form is imposed by the fitted law, not tested.
No depth/width or shape comparison at fixed parameters.
Image, video and other non-string modalities. No power-law fit for repeated data or fine-tuning.
No quantitative fit or prediction of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; trends are qualitative from bar plots.
Parameter counting, training schedule and fitting method are not varied.

missing.what: Table 1 per-representation fitted exponents α, β and in-grid MAE/RMSE (values garbled in extraction but needed to compare with Kaplan/Hoffmann exponents)
De novo metrics vs epochs (Table 2) and the temperature/top-k sweep at fixed weights, showing generation metrics do not track scale
Two-epoch vs one-epoch ΔL = L(P,2B) − L(P,B) sweep across representations

record.verdict_notes: The SAFE allocation direction is internally contradictory: Table 3 and Sec. 5.2 vs Table 4 and App. A.3–A.4. FragLink b = 512142 in Table 4 is an evident typo. Compute-optimal allocation is derived analytically from the fit, so the power-law allocation is assumed rather than measured. Downstream evidence is qualitative because the plots are unreadable. R19–R21 duplicate R12, R13, R15/R16. The V5 label in the record wrongly cited downstream rows; downstream LoRA results have no power-law fit.

versions.untested_parts: Tests molecular string models on the reported model-size, token-budget, and compute grid; does not test natural-language models or establish a universal law beyond the tested representations and ranges.
The paper plots extrapolated segments from fitted laws but does not validate predictions against independently trained runs orders of magnitude beyond the fitting grid.
Reports compute-optimal allocation and tokens-per-parameter trends, but does not independently validate the fitted optima on new runs outside the grid. SAFE results are internally inconsistent.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests molecular string representations and LoRA downstream transfer, not image/video or other modalities, nor fine-tuning as a pretraining-loss scaling regime.
Evaluates molecular property prediction after LoRA adaptation, not general language-model downstream tasks or a calibrated predictor from pretraining loss to downstream performance.

Shows representation-dependent trends and discusses repeated-corpus training, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, fitting method, or training schedule to isolate their effects. It does not test the cited disagreement between the original natural-language studies.

rows.measure: Held-out validation cross-entropy and fitted bivariate loss scaling; compute-optimal loss
rows.value: The paper reports a bivariate power-law fit and a smooth validation-loss landscape; Lopt decreases from 0.674047 to 0.551937 over the stated compute range.
rows.uncertainty: An empirical uncertainty scale from grid residuals is shown for the compute-controlled curves; no numerical error bar stated here.
rows.note: The paper says validation loss decreases with model size and data volume on the grid and describes the fitted law as adequate for compute-controlled analysis.
rows.check: The Lopt endpoint values are predictions from the fitted frontier (Table 3), not observed losses. The observed evidence is the grid losses (Fig. 6) and the in-grid fit errors (Table 1, garbled). Same issue for R2–R5.

rows.subject: DeepSMILES molecular language models
rows.stage_stated: from-scratch pretraining; single epoch grid used for fit
rows.operation_detail: Derive compute-optimal allocation from the fitted bivariate loss law under P D = C.
rows.measure: Optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio and compute-optimal validation loss
rows.value: ρopt decreases from 2.186 × 10^2 to 4.838 × 10^1; corr(log C, log ρopt) = −1.000. Lopt decreases from 0.674047 to 0.551937.
rows.note: The paper interprets the decreasing ratio as a progressively more parameter-heavy optimum.
rows.check: corr(log C, log ρopt) = −1.000 follows from the fitted functional form (ρ ∝ C^((α−β)/(α+β))). It is not an independent check that the allocation is a stable power. The optimum is not validated by new runs. Same for R7, R8, R10.

rows.operation_detail: Train for multiple epochs on an unchanged tokenized corpus and measure end-of-epoch validation loss.

conditions.value: up to 5; SMILES 100M setting up to 10

rows.measure: Held-out validation cross-entropy as effective training tokens and compute increase through corpus replay
rows.baseline: single-epoch run on the same corpus
rows.value: Validation loss generally falls with additional epochs, but gains diminish; later passes can show mild fluctuations. The authors say repeated passes are not equivalent to acquiring new tokens.
rows.note: This is an auxiliary repeated-data analysis, not the basis of the primary scaling fits.
rows.check: This is a repeated-data regime. It is not V1's setting, where tokens are not the bottleneck, so the V1 link is removed. It bears on V5 (repeated data), but no power law is fitted: loss falls with epochs, with diminishing gains and fluctuations.
